sets.skill: Analyzing Figurative, Connotative, and Technical Language

questions.stem: "The sky cried all afternoon" is an example of what kind of language?
options: figurative language
technical language
a true, literal statement
a scientific fact
questions.why: The sky cannot literally cry; this is figurative language (personification) describing rain.

questions.stem: Which type of language describes a word's dictionary definition with no feeling attached?
options: literal language
connotative language
figurative language
poetic language
questions.why: Literal language states the plain, factual meaning of a word.

questions.stem: The word "photosynthesis" is an example of what kind of language?
options: technical language
figurative language
connotative language
casual slang
questions.why: "Photosynthesis" is a specialized, field-specific term, which makes it technical language.

questions.stem: "Her smile was a ray of sunshine" uses what kind of language?
options: figurative language
technical language
a literal fact
a scientific term
questions.why: A smile cannot literally be a ray of sunshine; this is a figurative comparison (metaphor).

questions.stem: Which word carries a more negative connotation than the neutral word "thin"?
options: skinny
slender
narrow
lean
questions.why: "Skinny" often carries a more negative, unflattering feeling than the neutral word "thin."

questions.stem: Which word carries a more positive connotation than the neutral word "thin"?
options: slender
scrawny
bony
gaunt
questions.why: "Slender" suggests a graceful, positive quality, unlike the other more negative words.

questions.stem: The term "algorithm" used in a computer science class is an example of what kind of language?
options: technical language
figurative language
connotative language
exaggeration
questions.why: "Algorithm" is a specialized term used in a particular field, making it technical language.

questions.stem: "The news hit her like a ton of bricks" is an example of what kind of language?
options: figurative language
literal language
technical language
a plain fact
questions.why: News cannot literally weigh like bricks; this is a figurative comparison describing shock.

questions.stem: Which best defines "connotative language"?
options: language that carries an emotional feeling beyond its dictionary meaning
language that states only scientific facts
language that is always spoken, never written
language that has no meaning at all
questions.why: Connotative language carries an emotional or associative feeling beyond the literal dictionary definition.

questions.stem: Which best defines "literal language"?
options: language that means exactly what it says, with no hidden or extra meaning
language that always exaggerates the truth
language used only by scientists
language that hides its true meaning on purpose
questions.why: Literal language means exactly what it says, without any figurative or hidden meaning.

questions.stem: In a biology class, the word "cross-examine" would NOT be considered technical because it belongs to which field instead?
options: law
biology
chemistry
physics
questions.why: "Cross-examine" is a technical term from the field of law, not biology.

questions.stem: "The old house groaned in the wind" is an example of what kind of language?
options: figurative language
literal language
technical language
a true scientific fact
questions.why: A house cannot literally groan; this figurative language (personification) describes creaking sounds.

questions.stem: Which word has a more positive connotation than the neutral word "old"?
options: vintage
ancient
decrepit
outdated
questions.why: "Vintage" suggests something valuable or charming, giving it a more positive connotation than "old."

questions.stem: Which word has a more negative connotation than the neutral word "old"?
options: decrepit
classic
vintage
mature
questions.why: "Decrepit" suggests something worn out and falling apart, giving it a negative connotation.

questions.stem: The term "photosynthesis" would most likely appear in which kind of text?
options: a science textbook
a poem about love
a recipe for cookies
a sports article
questions.why: "Photosynthesis" is a technical biology term, so it would most likely appear in a science textbook.

questions.stem: "Time is a thief" is an example of what kind of language?
options: figurative language
literal language
technical language
a plain fact
questions.why: Time cannot literally steal; this is a figurative comparison (metaphor) suggesting time takes things away.

questions.stem: Which choice best explains the difference between "literal" and "figurative" language?
options: literal language means exactly what it says; figurative language means something beyond the actual words
literal language is always longer than figurative language
figurative language is only used in science writing
there is no real difference between the two
questions.why: Literal language states the plain meaning, while figurative language suggests a meaning beyond the literal words.

questions.stem: "Cross-examine," "verdict," and "testimony" are examples of what kind of language?
options: technical language from the field of law
figurative language from poetry
connotative language about feelings
slang used only by teenagers
questions.why: These words are specialized terms used in the legal field, making them technical language.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses figurative language?
options: The stars winked at the sleepy travelers below.
The thermometer read ten degrees this morning.
The library opens at nine o'clock.
The recipe calls for two cups of flour.
questions.why: Stars cannot literally wink; this is figurative language (personification).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses only literal language, with no figurative meaning?
options: The bus arrives at the corner every morning at eight.
The wind whispered secrets through the trees.
Her words cut deeper than any knife.
The classroom was a zoo during the fire drill.
questions.why: This sentence states a plain fact about the bus schedule with no figurative language.

questions.stem: A word's "connotation" refers to what?
options: the feeling or association a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning
the exact number of letters in a word
the part of speech a word belongs to
the country where a word was invented
questions.why: Connotation is the emotional feeling or association attached to a word beyond its literal definition.

questions.stem: Which of these is most likely a technical term used specifically in a weather report?
options: barometric pressure
a heart of gold
time flies
raining cats and dogs
questions.why: "Barometric pressure" is a specialized term used in meteorology (weather science).

questions.stem: "He was a lion in the fight" is an example of what kind of language?
options: figurative language
literal language
technical language
a plain fact
questions.why: He is not literally a lion; this figurative comparison (metaphor) suggests bravery or fierceness.

questions.stem: Which word choice would create a more negative feeling about a small living space, compared to "cozy"?
options: cramped
snug
compact
intimate
questions.why: "Cramped" suggests discomfort, giving it a more negative connotation than "cozy" or "snug."

questions.stem: Which word choice would create a more positive feeling about a small living space, compared to "cramped"?
options: cozy
tiny
cramped
squeezed
questions.why: "Cozy" suggests warmth and comfort, giving it a positive connotation unlike "cramped."

questions.stem: The phrase "the company's bottom line" uses "bottom line" as what kind of language?
options: technical business language meaning final profit or loss
figurative language about the ocean floor
connotative language about feelings
a casual nickname with no real meaning
questions.why: In business, "bottom line" is a technical term referring to a company's final profit or loss.

questions.stem: Which sentence best shows the use of a technical term from the field of medicine?
options: The doctor measured the patient's blood pressure before the exam.
The patient's heart was a drum pounding with fear.
The waiting room felt like a prison cell.
Her smile was sunshine on a cloudy day.
questions.why: "Blood pressure" is a specialized medical term, making this sentence an example of technical language.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses connotative language to make a crowded room sound unpleasant, rather than simply full?
options: The room was packed, with bodies pressed against every wall.
The room contained thirty people at the time of the meeting.
The room measured twenty feet by thirty feet.
The room had four windows facing the courtyard.
questions.why: "Packed, with bodies pressed" carries a negative, uncomfortable feeling beyond the literal fact of a full room.

questions.stem: A news article states, "The defendant's testimony was examined during cross-examination." Which words are technical, field-specific vocabulary?
options: testimony and cross-examination
defendant's and was
during and the
stated and article
questions.why: "Testimony" and "cross-examination" are specialized legal terms, making them technical vocabulary.

questions.stem: Which revision replaces a neutral word with one that has a more positive connotation, without changing the literal meaning?
options: The chef served a generous portion of the stew.
The chef served a large portion of the stew.
The chef served an excessive portion of the stew.
The chef served a bloated portion of the stew.
questions.why: "Generous" carries a warm, positive connotation, while still meaning roughly the same amount as "large."

questions.stem: Which sentence below is figurative rather than literal?
options: The mountain stood guard over the quiet valley.
The mountain rose eight thousand feet above sea level.
The mountain was covered in snow by October.
The mountain had three marked hiking trails.
questions.why: A mountain cannot literally "stand guard"; this is figurative language (personification).

questions.stem: A biology textbook defines "photosynthesis" as the process by which plants convert light into energy. What kind of language is "photosynthesis"?
options: technical language specific to the field of biology
figurative language comparing plants to people
connotative language with a negative feeling
slang used informally among students
questions.why: "Photosynthesis" is a precise, specialized term used in biology, making it technical language.

questions.stem: Which pair of words has the same basic (literal/denotative) meaning but different connotations?
options: childlike and childish
run and jump
happy and chair
quickly and slowly
questions.why: "Childlike" and "childish" both relate to children, but "childlike" feels positive (innocent) while "childish" feels negative (immature).

questions.stem: In the sentence "The negotiations collapsed overnight," what is the effect of the word "collapsed" rather than "ended"?
options: it suggests a sudden, dramatic failure rather than a calm, neutral stop
it suggests the negotiations succeeded completely
it has no effect on the tone of the sentence at all
it is a technical legal term with no emotional weight
questions.why: "Collapsed" has a connotation of sudden, dramatic failure, unlike the neutral word "ended."

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a technical term that a reader unfamiliar with cooking might not immediately understand?
options: The chef began to julienne the carrots for the salad.
The chef chopped the carrots into small pieces.
The chef added the carrots to the boiling water.
The chef washed the carrots before cooking.
questions.why: "Julienne" is a specialized cooking term for cutting vegetables into thin strips, making it technical vocabulary.

questions.stem: What effect does the word "ancient" have, compared to the neutral word "old," when describing a tradition?
options: it adds a sense of deep respect and long history
it suggests the tradition is broken and useless
it removes all meaning from the sentence
it is a purely technical scientific term
questions.why: "Ancient" carries a connotation of deep history and respect, stronger than the neutral word "old."

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a metaphor, a type of figurative language that says one thing IS another?
options: Her courage was a shield against every insult.
Her courage helped her face every insult calmly.
Her courage was measured by a psychologist.
Her courage grew slowly over several years.
questions.why: Saying courage "was a shield" directly equates two unlike things, which is the definition of a metaphor.

questions.stem: In the passage, what does the phrase "felt like a boulder" figuratively suggest about Mina's backpack?
options: it felt extremely heavy and burdensome
it was literally made of stone
it was unusually light and easy to carry
it had been left behind at school
questions.why: "Felt like a boulder" is a figurative comparison (simile) suggesting the backpack felt very heavy.
questions.passage: Mina stood at the empty bus stop as the last light drained from the sky. Her backpack felt like a boulder on her shoulders. When the bus finally groaned around the corner, relief washed over her like a warm wave.

questions.stem: In the passage, the bus is described as "groaned around the corner." What kind of language is this?
options: figurative language (personification), giving the bus a human-like sound
technical language describing a mechanical part
a literal description of a human voice
connotative language with a cheerful feeling
questions.why: Buses cannot literally groan; this is figurative language (personification) describing the bus's noise.
questions.passage: Mina stood at the empty bus stop as the last light drained from the sky. Her backpack felt like a boulder on her shoulders. When the bus finally groaned around the corner, relief washed over her like a warm wave.

questions.stem: In the passage, "relief washed over her like a warm wave" is an example of what kind of figurative language?
options: a simile, comparing relief to a wave using "like"
a technical term from ocean science
a literal description of actual water
a negative connotation of comfort
questions.why: This is a simile because it compares relief to a wave using the word "like."
questions.passage: Mina stood at the empty bus stop as the last light drained from the sky. Her backpack felt like a boulder on her shoulders. When the bus finally groaned around the corner, relief washed over her like a warm wave.

questions.stem: Which word or phrase in the passage is a technical term from science class?
options: cellular respiration
double-checked
trembled
speak for itself
questions.why: "Cellular respiration" is a specialized biology term, making it technical language.
questions.passage: Before the judges arrived, Hana double-checked her poster on cellular respiration. She had labeled each diagram carefully, hoping the evidence of her experiment would speak for itself. Still, her hands trembled like leaves in a storm.

questions.stem: What does "her hands trembled like leaves in a storm" figuratively suggest about Hana?
options: she was extremely nervous
she was literally standing outside in bad weather
she was completely calm and confident
she had just finished exercising
questions.why: This simile compares her trembling hands to leaves in a storm, suggesting intense nervousness.
questions.passage: Before the judges arrived, Hana double-checked her poster on cellular respiration. She had labeled each diagram carefully, hoping the evidence of her experiment would speak for itself. Still, her hands trembled like leaves in a storm.

questions.stem: What effect does the phrase "the evidence would speak for itself" have, compared to simply saying "the evidence was good"?
options: it personifies the evidence, suggesting it is powerful enough to convince on its own
it is a technical scientific term with no figurative meaning
it suggests the evidence was weak and unconvincing
it has no connotation or figurative meaning at all
questions.why: "Speak for itself" personifies the evidence, giving it human qualities to emphasize its persuasive strength.
questions.passage: Before the judges arrived, Hana double-checked her poster on cellular respiration. She had labeled each diagram carefully, hoping the evidence of her experiment would speak for itself. Still, her hands trembled like leaves in a storm.

questions.stem: A word's connotation can change the emotional feeling of a sentence even when its literal, dictionary meaning stays the same.
questions.why: Connotation adds emotional weight beyond the literal meaning, which can shift how a sentence feels.

questions.stem: Technical language is meant to be understood easily by anyone, regardless of their background knowledge.
questions.why: Technical language is often specialized and may be unclear to readers unfamiliar with that particular field.

questions.stem: Figurative language always states the plain, literal truth about a situation.
questions.why: Figurative language suggests meaning beyond the literal words; it does not state a plain, literal truth.

questions.stem: Match each example to the correct type of language.

pairs.left: "Her anger boiled over during the meeting."
"The mitochondria produce energy for the cell."
"The apartment felt cozy rather than cramped."

questions.why: Each phrase demonstrates a different type of language: figurative comparison, specialized vocabulary, and emotional word choice.

questions.stem: Which sentence below best demonstrates connotative language shaping a reader's opinion of a character?
options: The stubborn old man refused every offer of help.
The elderly man was seventy-two years old.
The man lived alone in a small house.
The man walked to the store every Tuesday.
questions.why: "Stubborn" carries a negative connotation that shapes the reader's opinion of the character, beyond a neutral fact.

questions.stem: A weather report uses the term "barometric pressure." Why might the reporter also explain this term in simpler words?
options: because it is technical language that general audiences may not fully understand
because it is figurative language with a hidden meaning
because it is slang used only by teenagers
because it has no real meaning in meteorology
questions.why: "Barometric pressure" is technical vocabulary from meteorology, so a reporter may clarify it for general audiences.

questions.stem: Which revised sentence uses a word with a more negative connotation than the original word "careful"?
options: The paranoid driver checked his mirrors every few seconds.
The careful driver checked his mirrors every few seconds.
The attentive driver checked his mirrors every few seconds.
The cautious driver checked his mirrors every few seconds.
questions.why: "Paranoid" suggests excessive, unhealthy worry, giving it a more negative connotation than "careful."

questions.stem: Which sentence below contains an example of a symbol, where an object represents a larger idea?
options: The dove on the flag represented the nation's hope for peace.
The flag was made of cotton and dyed bright red.
The flag measured six feet by four feet.
The flag was raised at exactly eight in the morning.
questions.why: The dove functions as a symbol, representing the larger idea of peace rather than just a literal bird.

questions.stem: In the sentence "The debate team dismantled their opponent's argument piece by piece," what is the effect of "dismantled"?
options: it suggests a thorough, methodical defeat, as if taking apart a machine
it suggests the argument was never actually discussed
it is a neutral, purely technical engineering term with no figurative use here
it suggests the debate team lost badly
questions.why: "Dismantled" figuratively compares defeating an argument to taking apart a machine piece by piece, suggesting a thorough defeat.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a technical term from the field of music rather than everyday vocabulary?
options: The conductor asked the orchestra to play the next passage in a slow tempo marked largo.
The conductor asked the orchestra to play the next part more quietly.
The conductor stood at the front of the stage with a baton.
The conductor smiled as the audience applauded loudly.
questions.why: "Tempo" and "largo" are specialized musical terms, making this sentence an example of technical language.

questions.stem: In the sentence "The committee's decision cast a shadow over the celebration," what does "cast a shadow" figuratively suggest?
options: it dampened or darkened the mood of an otherwise happy event
it literally blocked sunlight from reaching the celebration
it is a technical term used in photography
it suggests the celebration became brighter and more joyful
questions.why: "Cast a shadow" is a figurative expression suggesting something darkened or dampened the mood of an event.

questions.stem: In the passage, "the small town had become a fortress of ice" is best described as what kind of language, and what does it suggest?
options: figurative language suggesting the town felt cold, isolated, and difficult to penetrate
technical language describing an actual military structure
literal language describing a real fortress built from ice blocks
connotative language with an entirely positive, warm feeling
questions.why: This is figurative language (metaphor) suggesting the town felt isolated and harshly cold, like a fortress of ice.
questions.passage: By February, the small town had become a fortress of ice. Pipes froze overnight, and even conversations seemed to crystallize in the cold air. Mr. Aziz, the baker, kept insisting that spring was only a heartbeat away, though no one quite believed him anymore.

questions.stem: What is the effect of saying conversations "seemed to crystallize in the cold air" rather than simply "people stopped talking"?
options: it figuratively suggests words becoming sharp, brittle, and frozen in place, emphasizing the harshness of the cold
it is a purely technical scientific description of actual crystal formation
it suggests people were talking more cheerfully than usual
it has no figurative meaning and simply states a plain fact
questions.why: This figurative use of "crystallize" suggests words becoming frozen and brittle, emphasizing the oppressive cold more vividly than a plain statement.
questions.passage: By February, the small town had become a fortress of ice. Pipes froze overnight, and even conversations seemed to crystallize in the cold air. Mr. Aziz, the baker, kept insisting that spring was only a heartbeat away, though no one quite believed him anymore.

questions.stem: Why might the author choose the phrase "only a heartbeat away" instead of "coming soon" to describe spring's arrival?
options: it connects spring's arrival to something alive and urgent, adding emotional hope despite the townspeople's doubt
it is a technical medical term describing cardiac rhythm
it suggests spring is actually very far away
it removes all emotional meaning from the sentence
questions.why: "A heartbeat away" figuratively connects spring to something alive and immediate, adding a hopeful emotional tone that contrasts with the townspeople's doubt.
questions.passage: By February, the small town had become a fortress of ice. Pipes froze overnight, and even conversations seemed to crystallize in the cold air. Mr. Aziz, the baker, kept insisting that spring was only a heartbeat away, though no one quite believed him anymore.

questions.stem: Which words in the passage are technical, field-specific vocabulary from the legal system?
options: cross-examination, testimony, and verdict
sharper, steady, and forward
attorney's and witness's
grew and began
questions.why: "Cross-examination," "testimony," and "verdict" are specialized legal terms, making them technical vocabulary.
questions.passage: The attorney's cross-examination grew sharper with each question. The witness's testimony, once steady, began to splinter under the pressure, and the jury leaned forward as if sensing the verdict shift.

questions.stem: In the passage, the testimony is described as beginning "to splinter under the pressure." What does this figurative use of "splinter" suggest?
options: the witness's once-steady account was starting to break apart and become inconsistent
the witness literally touched a piece of broken wood during questioning
the testimony became stronger and more convincing
the jury fell asleep during the questioning
questions.why: Figuratively, "splinter" suggests the testimony was breaking apart into inconsistent pieces under pressure, not literal wood breaking.
questions.passage: The attorney's cross-examination grew sharper with each question. The witness's testimony, once steady, began to splinter under the pressure, and the jury leaned forward as if sensing the verdict shift.

questions.stem: What is the combined effect of pairing technical legal vocabulary with figurative language like "splinter" in this passage?
options: it grounds the scene in a real courtroom setting while also conveying the emotional tension of the moment
it makes the passage purely informational, with no emotional tone at all
it confuses the reader by mixing unrelated topics with no purpose
it removes any sense of tension from the courtroom scene
questions.why: Combining technical vocabulary with figurative language grounds the scene realistically while still conveying emotional tension through vivid imagery.
questions.passage: The attorney's cross-examination grew sharper with each question. The witness's testimony, once steady, began to splinter under the pressure, and the jury leaned forward as if sensing the verdict shift.

questions.stem: A reviewer writes, "The algorithm elegantly solves the problem in record time." Which word in this sentence is technical, and which carries connotation?
options: "algorithm" is technical; "elegantly" carries a positive connotation
"elegantly" is technical; "algorithm" carries a positive connotation
both words are purely literal with no connotation or technical meaning
neither word has any specialized or emotional meaning
questions.why: "Algorithm" is a specialized computer science term, while "elegantly" adds a positive emotional judgment beyond the literal meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence best demonstrates how connotation can shift a reader's sympathy toward a character, even though the literal facts stay the same?
options: The old woman shuffled slowly, her frail hands trembling with every step.
The woman, age seventy-eight, walked at a reduced pace.
The woman walked from the kitchen to the front door.
The woman's house had three bedrooms and two bathrooms.
questions.why: Words like "shuffled," "frail," and "trembling" carry connotations of vulnerability, shifting sympathy, even though the underlying fact (an old woman walking slowly) is the same.

questions.stem: A critic says a poem's imagery is "crystal," while its central metaphor is "murky." What is the critic most likely contrasting?
options: sharp, clear description versus a confusing, unclear comparison
two equally confusing elements of the poem
two equally clear elements of the poem
the poem's rhyme scheme versus its punctuation
questions.why: "Crystal" figuratively suggests clarity, while "murky" figuratively suggests confusion, so the critic is contrasting clear imagery with an unclear metaphor.

questions.stem: Why would an author use the technical term "photosynthesis" rather than a vague phrase like "plants making food" in a nature documentary script?
options: precision and credibility matter in scientific explanations, and the technical term conveys exact meaning
technical terms always confuse viewers, so they should never be used
vague phrases are always more scientifically accurate than technical terms
there is no difference in meaning between the two phrases
questions.why: A technical term like "photosynthesis" offers precise, credible meaning appropriate for scientific explanation, unlike a vague paraphrase.

questions.stem: In the sentence "The negotiations were a chess match, each side calculating its next move," which best explains the figurative language?
options: an extended metaphor compares the negotiation process to a strategic game
a technical term from the field of chess competition rules
a literal description of an actual chess match taking place
connotative language with no figurative comparison at all
questions.why: This is an extended metaphor comparing the negotiation process to a chess match, emphasizing strategy and calculation.

questions.stem: A speech uses the connotative phrase "the backbone of our community" to describe local teachers. What does this figurative phrase suggest about teachers?
options: they provide essential support and structure that holds the community together
they are literally part of the human skeletal system
they are the weakest, least important members of the community
they have no real impact on the community at all
questions.why: "Backbone" figuratively suggests teachers provide essential, structural support, much like a backbone supports a body.

questions.stem: Which choice best explains the difference in effect between describing rain as "a gentle mist" versus "a relentless downpour"?
options: the first connotes calm and softness, while the second connotes overwhelming, unstoppable force
both phrases are purely literal with identical connotations
the first is technical language, and the second is figurative language
there is no meaningful difference between the two phrases
questions.why: "Gentle mist" connotes softness and calm, while "relentless downpour" connotes overwhelming force, even though both describe rain.

questions.stem: A scientist explains, "The data's margin of error undermines the study's conclusions." Which phrase is technical, field-specific language from statistics?
options: margin of error
undermines the study's
the data's
conclusions
questions.why: "Margin of error" is a specialized statistical term, making it technical language from that field.

questions.stem: Why might an author deliberately combine technical vocabulary with figurative language in a single passage about a hospital?
options: to ground the scene in medical realism while still conveying the emotional weight of the situation
to confuse the reader with no clear purpose
to remove all emotional content from the passage entirely
technical and figurative language can never appear together in good writing
questions.why: Combining technical vocabulary with figurative language can ground a scene in realism while still conveying emotional depth.

questions.stem: A columnist writes that a rival's proposal is "all bark and no bite." What does this figurative idiom suggest?
options: the proposal sounds aggressive or impressive but has little real effect or substance
the proposal was created by a dog trainer
the proposal was extremely effective and powerful
the proposal contained detailed technical specifications
questions.why: "All bark and no bite" is a figurative idiom suggesting something seems threatening or impressive but lacks real substance or effect.

questions.stem: Which sentence best shows a word's connotation reinforcing the overall tone of determination in a paragraph about an athlete?
options: She refused to quit, relentlessly pushing through every grueling mile of the marathon.
She ran a marathon that was twenty-six point two miles long.
She finished the race in four hours and twelve minutes.
She wore running shoes and a blue headband during the race.
questions.why: Words like "refused," "relentlessly," and "grueling" carry connotations of determination, reinforcing the paragraph's tone.

questions.stem: A business report states the company's "net profit margin" declined. Which best explains why this phrase is technical rather than figurative?
options: it refers to a precise, calculable financial measurement used specifically in business and accounting
it compares the company to a living creature in a figurative way
it uses a metaphor to describe the company's emotional state
it has no specific or specialized meaning in any field
questions.why: "Net profit margin" is a precise, calculable financial term used specifically in accounting, making it technical rather than figurative.

questions.stem: Which revision best demonstrates how changing a single word's connotation can shift a sentence from sounding like praise to sounding like criticism?
options: "The manager was assertive" versus "The manager was aggressive," describing the same behavior
"The manager arrived" versus "The employee arrived," describing different people
"The manager left early" versus "The manager left late," describing different times
"The manager spoke" versus "The manager wrote," describing different actions
questions.why: "Assertive" and "aggressive" can describe the same behavior but carry very different connotations, shifting the sentence from praise to criticism.

questions.stem: A nature writer describes a hawk's dive as "a blade cutting through the sky." What is the effect of this figurative comparison?
options: it emphasizes the hawk's sharp, swift, and precise movement
it is a literal description of an actual blade falling from the sky
it is a technical term used in ornithology to classify hawk species
it suggests the hawk moved slowly and clumsily
questions.why: Comparing the hawk's dive to a blade figuratively emphasizes its sharp, swift, and precise movement.

questions.stem: In the passage, describing the opponent's statement as "a loaded gun" is an example of what kind of language, and what does it suggest?
options: figurative language suggesting the statement was dangerously sharp and ready to do damage
technical language describing an actual firearm used in the debate
literal language stating that a real weapon was present in the room
connotative language suggesting the statement was calm and gentle
questions.why: This figurative comparison suggests the opponent's statement felt dangerously sharp and ready to strike, not a literal weapon.
questions.passage: As the final round began, Jo felt the room's energy sharpen into something electric. Her opponent's opening statement was a loaded gun, every word aimed with precision. Jo took a breath and reminded herself that preparation, not panic, was her only real ammunition.

questions.stem: Why does the author extend the metaphor by having Jo think of "preparation" as her "ammunition"?
options: it continues the battle imagery, showing Jo reframing her own strength in the same figurative terms as the threat she faces
it introduces a new, unrelated technical term from a different field
it suggests Jo is literally carrying a weapon into the debate
it removes all figurative meaning established earlier in the passage
questions.why: Extending the "weapon" metaphor to Jo's preparation shows her reframing her own strength using the same figurative battle imagery.
questions.passage: As the final round began, Jo felt the room's energy sharpen into something electric. Her opponent's opening statement was a loaded gun, every word aimed with precision. Jo took a breath and reminded herself that preparation, not panic, was her only real ammunition.

questions.stem: What does the phrase "the room's energy sharpen into something electric" suggest about the mood in the passage?
options: the atmosphere became tense, charged, and intensely focused

questions.passageTitle: The Woman Who Mapped the Ocean Floor
questions.passage:
Marie Tharp spent most of the 1950s hunched over data tables, translating raw sonar readings into hand-drawn profiles of the ocean floor. At the time, women were not permitted on the research ships that collected the data — so Tharp did her work entirely from land, relying on measurements gathered by her male colleagues at sea. Piece by piece, she assembled a picture no one had ever seen before.

In 1953, Tharp noticed something strange in her calculations: a deep, V-shaped valley running down the center of a long underwater mountain range. She believed it was a rift valley — evidence that the ocean floor was spreading apart. Her research partner initially dismissed the idea as "girl talk," since it contradicted the accepted theory of the time. But Tharp kept mapping. Her charts, later published in 1977 as the World Ocean Floor Panorama, provided crucial visual evidence for what would become the theory of plate tectonics — now a cornerstone of modern geology.

Deshawn stared at the tangle of wires spilling out of the old radio. His grandfather had given it to him that morning, saying only, "See if you can bring it back to life." Deshawn had never fixed anything more complicated than a bicycle chain.

He turned the radio over in his hands, studying the screws, the cracked dial, the frayed cord. Then he set it down and pulled a notebook from his backpack, sketching the inside of the radio from memory before he'd even opened it.

An hour passed. Then two. Deshawn's stomach growled, but he barely noticed. He tested one wire, then another, muttering to himself each time something didn't work. When a spark suddenly jumped from the battery terminal, he yelped and dropped his screwdriver — but a moment later, he picked it back up.

By evening, the dial was still cracked, but a faint hum came from the speaker. Deshawn grinned and ran to find his grandfather.
